title: Evidence uncertainty and decision guarantees in investment research
markdown:
## 1 Feature attribution and the value of verification [SHAP](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.07874) decomposes a model prediction into additive feature contributions through its local accuracy property. Conditional Shapley methods account for dependence among features, and Rashomon-set methods assess the stability of explanations across near-optimal models ([SHAP](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.07874); [Aas et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/1903.10464v3); [Marx et al.](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v206/marx23a.html)). These methods do not establish whether the corporate inputs $`x`$ are factually correct. In investment diligence, where self-reported disclosures may contain AI-polished greenwashing, an analyst also needs to know which corrections to the evidence could change a decision. For a linear scoring model with a fixed marginal background distribution $`Q`$, the [SHAP](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.07874) attribution for feature $`j`$ is $`\phi_j = \beta_j(x_j - E_Q X_j)`$. Suppose the feature has unresolved factual uncertainty bounded by $`|\delta_j| \le d_j`$. Its sensitivity to verification is $`|\beta_j|d_j`$. Over a box of admissible evidence errors, the exact worst-case change in the company score is $$ \sup_{|\delta_j| \le d_j} |f(x + \delta) - f(x)| = \sum_j |\beta_j| d_j $$ The triangle inequality gives the upper bound. It is attained by choosing the endpoint of each error interval so that every perturbation moves the score in the same direction. Attribution magnitude and verification value therefore require separate calculations: • A financial metric may have a large [SHAP](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.07874) attribution $`|\phi_j|`$ and come from audited filings that have already been verified ($`d_j \approx 0`$). Further checks of that field contribute little to reducing score uncertainty. • A self-reported ESG or operating metric may lie near the sector mean ($`x_j \approx E_Q X_j \implies \phi_j \approx 0`$), giving it a near-zero [SHAP](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.07874) attribution. Substantial unresolved reporting error ($`d_j \gg 0`$) may nevertheless be sufficient to reverse a company ranking. Resampling existing records cannot, by itself, identify a shared reporting or AI-marketing bias. Suppose $`n`$ reported observations satisfy $`X_i = \mu + b + \varepsilon_i`$, where $`\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)`$ are independent errors and $`b \neq 0`$ is an unmodeled bias common to all records. Examples include systematic overstatement across a sector or coordinated AI-assisted public relations. A conventional nominal 95% normal confidence interval centered on the sample mean $`\bar{X}`$ covers the true parameter $`\mu`$ with probability $$ \Pr\left\{ \mu \in \left[ \bar{X} - z\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}, \ \bar{X} + z\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \right] \right\} = \Phi\left( z - \frac{b\sqrt{n}}{\sigma} \right) - \Phi\left( -z - \frac{b\sqrt{n}}{\sigma} \right) \longrightarrow 0 \quad (\text{as } n \to \infty) $$ where $`z = \Phi^{-1}(0.975) \approx 1.96`$. With a fixed nonzero common bias, increasing the sample size ($`n \to \infty`$) reduces random variance while the interval's coverage of the true parameter tends to zero. Bootstrapping the same biased records supplies no information that identifies $`b`$. External evidence is needed to bound the common bias, and ranking analysis must retain the resulting uncertainty. ## 2 Joint uncertainty over models and evidence The framework represents model multiplicity and unresolved evidence jointly to assess whether an ESG or investment ranking remains stable under admissible changes to either. Fix the prediction target, input definitions, and output scale. Let $`\mathcal{F}_0`$ contain $`M`$ candidate scoring models specified before examining the validation data. The validation set consists of $`n`$ i.i.d. observations from the target evaluation distribution, independent of model construction, and the loss is bounded in $`[0, 1]`$. For a failure probability $`\alpha \in (0, 1)`$, Hoeffding's inequality and a union bound give $$ \Pr\left\{ \max_{f \in \mathcal{F}_0} |\hat{L}_n(f) - L(f)| \le t_n \right\} \ge 1 - \alpha, \qquad t_n = \sqrt{\frac{\log(2M / \alpha)}{2n}} $$ Let $`f^*`$ minimize population loss within $`\mathcal{F}_0`$. Retaining all models whose empirical validation loss is within $`2t_n`$ of the empirical minimum defines an empirical Rashomon set: $$ \mathcal{F}_\alpha = \left\{ f \in \mathcal{F}_0 : \hat{L}_n(f) \le \min_{g \in \mathcal{F}_0} \hat{L}_n(g) + 2t_n \right\} $$ On the simultaneous concentration event, $`\hat{L}_n(f^*) \le L(f^*) + t_n \le \min_g \hat{L}_n(g) + 2t_n`$. Thus $`f^* \in \mathcal{F}_\alpha`$, and every retained model has population excess loss at most $`4t_n`$ ([Marx et al.](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v206/marx23a.html)). The evidence uncertainty set $`\mathcal{X}(E)`$ represents unresolved questions under the current diligence state $`E`$: entity boundaries, reporting periods, physical units, measurement definitions, shared third-party sources, and suspected greenwashing claims. Each $`X \in \mathcal{X}(E)`$ specifies a joint input configuration for all candidate companies, preserving error dependence across companies and fields. Over the joint space $`\Omega(E) = \mathcal{F}_\alpha \times \mathcal{X}(E)`$, the exact worst-case bounds on the score difference between companies $`i`$ and $`k`$ are $$ \underline{\Delta}_{ik} = \inf_{(f, X) \in \Omega(E)} [f(x_i) - f(x_k)], \qquad \overline{\Delta}_{ik} = \sup_{(f, X) \in \Omega(E)} [f(x_i) - f(x_k)] $$ If $`\underline{\Delta}_{ik} > 0`$, the ordering $`i \succ k`$ holds for every retained model in $`\mathcal{F}_\alpha`$ and every admissible resolution of the evidence in $`\mathcal{X}(E)`$. Suppose calibration establishes that $`\mathcal{X}(E)`$ contains the true inputs with probability at least $`1 - \beta`$ at the specified certification stage. A union bound then gives joint inclusion of $`f^*`$ and the true inputs with probability at least $`1 - \alpha - \beta`$. The unconditional probability of issuing a certificate that is false for $`f^*`$ at the true inputs is therefore at most $`\alpha + \beta`$. Independence between model validation and evidence calibration is unnecessary. The guarantee concerns the best model in the prespecified class; it does not establish that the class is adequate or guarantee realized investment outcomes. Adaptive certification repeated over several stages requires calibration that is jointly valid across those stages. ## 3 Computing comparison bounds with support functions Convex support functions make the joint comparison bounds tractable ([Ben-Tal and Nemirovski](https://www2.isye.gatech.edu/~nemirovs/MOR_RCO_1998.pdf)). Let $`u \in U`$ collect unresolved factual quantities, including common benchmark errors and company-specific allowances for reporting error, and write company inputs as $`x_i(u) = \bar{x}_i + B_i u`$. For an affine scoring model, the pairwise difference is $`\Delta_f(u) = m_f + a_f^\top u`$, where $`a_f = (B_i - B_k)^\top \beta_f`$. The support function $`h_U(a) = \sup_{u \in U} a^\top u`$ gives exact comparison bounds: $$ \inf_{u \in U} \Delta_f(u) = m_f - h_U(-a_f), \qquad \sup_{u \in U} \Delta_f(u) = m_f + h_U(a_f) $$ For the ellipsoidal uncertainty set $`U = \{Cz : \|z\|_2 \le r\}`$, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives $`h_U(a_f) = r\|C^\top a_f\|_2`$. For an $`\ell_\infty`$ box centered at zero, $`h_U(a_f)`$ reduces to a weighted sum of absolute values. The joint representation allows shared errors to cancel exactly in a pairwise comparison. Let $`S`$ index common-source coordinates on which the two companies have identical loadings, so that $`(B_i-B_k)_{:,S}=0`$. Under the same linear scoring model, $$ (a_f)_S=0,\qquad \Delta_f(u)=m_f+(a_f)_{S^c}^{\top}u_{S^c} $$ The common-source contribution cancels; company-specific uncertainty remains in the support-function bound. If every uncertain direction cancels, $`a_f=0`$ and $`h_U(\pm a_f)=0`$. Subtracting intervals constructed separately for companies $`i`$ and $`k`$ permits a shared source to move in opposite directions at the same time. That combination is incompatible with the joint error structure and produces an unnecessarily wide difference bound. For a smooth nonlinear model, set $`m_f=\Delta_f(0)`$ and $`a_f=\nabla\Delta_f(0)`$. If $`\Delta_f(u)`$ is twice continuously differentiable on $`\|u\|_2 \le r`$ and its Hessian has operator norm bounded by $`K_f`$, Taylor's theorem gives $$ |\Delta_f(u) - m_f - a_f^\top u| \le \kappa_f, \qquad \kappa_f = \frac{1}{2}K_f r^2 \implies \underline{\Delta}_f \ge m_f - r\|a_f\|_2 - \kappa_f $$ For nonsmooth tree ensembles, leaf-region partitioning or mixed-integer linear programming provides bounds. The implementation prioritizes computation for company pairs whose difference bounds are close to the zero decision boundary. ## 4 Selecting queries by the regret they can remove When $`\underline{\Delta}_{ik} \le 0 < \overline{\Delta}_{ik}`$, the ranking is unresolved: a factual correction or resolution of ambiguous evidence could change the decision. The system prioritizes the next verification query $`q`$, such as reviewing a supplier contract, requesting original utility bills, or checking a regulatory filing. Let $`A`$ be a finite set of institutional actions, such as advancing company $`i`$ or company $`k`$ to final diligence, or deferring a rating. Let $`U(a, \omega)`$ be the prespecified utility of an action in scenario $`\omega \in \Omega`$, where $`\Omega`$ is nonempty and utilities are uniformly bounded. The baseline minimax regret over deterministic actions is $$ R^*(\Omega) = \min_{a \in A} \sup_{\omega \in \Omega} \left[ \max_{b \in A} U(b, \omega) - U(a, \omega) \right] $$ A query $`q`$ returns an observation $`o \in O_q`$ and restricts the compatible scenarios to a nonempty subset $`\Omega_{q,o} \subseteq \Omega`$. Its guaranteed reduction in worst-case decision regret is $$ V(q) = R^*(\Omega) - \sup_{o \in O_q} R^*(\Omega_{q,o}) \ge 0 $$ Nonnegativity follows from $`\Omega_{q,o} \subseteq \Omega`$: restricting the scenario set cannot increase worst-case regret for any fixed action, and minimizing over $`a \in A`$ preserves that inequality ([Robust Active Preference Elicitation](https://arxiv.org/html/2003.01899)). The calculation of $`V(q)`$ uses the set of compatible scenarios and requires no prior probability that a disclosure is exaggerated. At a fixed evidence state, maximizing $`V(q)`$ over affordable queries minimizes worst-case regret after one query. With positive, unequal costs $`c_q`$, the ratio $`V(q)/c_q`$ is a one-step efficiency heuristic. Complementary or sequential queries require joint or adaptive optimization under the total diligence budget $`B`$. ## 5 Propagating factual corrections through scores and attributions When diligence resolves a query and changes the verified evidence vector from $`x`$ to $`x'`$, the system follows versioned dependencies to recompute affected scores, peer rankings, and [SHAP](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.07874) explanations. With the scoring function $`f`$, background reference $`Q`$, and rubric version held fixed, Shapley efficiency gives the exact identity ([SHAP local accuracy](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1705.07874)): $$ f(x) = \phi_0 + \sum_j \phi_j(f, Q, x), \qquad \sum_j [\phi_j(f, Q, x') - \phi_j(f, Q, x)] = f(x') - f(x) $$ Suppose approximate Shapley outputs have efficiency residuals $`|\phi_0+\sum_j\phi_j-f(x)|\le\eta`$ and $`|\phi_0+\sum_j\phi'_j-f(x')|\le\eta'`$ under the same baseline $`\phi_0`$. The triangle inequality then gives the recomputation check $`|\sum_j \Delta \phi_j - \Delta f| \le \eta + \eta'`$. It verifies aggregate conservation, not the accuracy of individual attributions or the truth of the evidence. Every database update records `(field version, evidence document ID, model version, background Q, rubric version)`. These identifiers distinguish changes caused by factual corrections from those caused by model updates or changes to the background distribution. ## 6 Reproducible quantitative comparisons The following analytical benchmarks test the mechanisms under explicit model and parameter settings. 1. **Confidence interval coverage under common reporting bias.** • Set the shared bias to $`b = 0.2`$ and independent noise to $`\sigma = 1`$. If the common bias $`b`$ is ignored, a nominal 95% interval has actual coverage of 48.40% at $`n = 100`$ records and 0.000637% at $`n = 1,000`$. Once targeted verification establishes $`|b| \le 0.2`$, increasing the half-width to $`0.2 + 1.96/\sqrt{n}`$ gives 97.50% actual coverage. 2. **Cancellation of shared errors in pairwise rankings.** • Two companies have a nominal score difference of $`0.6`$ points and share an additive sector-benchmark error in $`[-1, 1]`$. Subtracting separately constructed company intervals gives $`[-1.4, 2.6]`$, which cannot certify the ordering. The joint support-function calculation cancels the shared error and gives $`[0.6, 0.6]`$, certifying the ranking. 3. **Minimax-regret verification compared with [SHAP](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.07874) magnitude.** • Consider a single query, with the same cost for each query option. The benchmark has 8 scenarios: 2 candidate models from the Rashomon set ($`s \in \{-1, 1\}`$) and 4 unresolved evidence configurations ($`z_1 \in \{-0.4, 0.4\}`$, $`z_2 \in \{-0.2, 0.2\}`$). The pairwise score difference is $`\Delta_s = 0.15s + z_1 + 0.3s z_2`$. A further shared feature has a large [SHAP](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.07874) attribution but is already verified ($`d_0 = 0`$). The action is to select company $`i`$ or company $`k`$, and regret is measured in model-score units.

Enumerating the eight scenarios shows that rechecking the verified field with a large [SHAP](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.07874) attribution produces no regret reduction ($`V(q) = 0`$). Verifying $`z_1`$ reduces worst-case regret from 0.61 to zero. In this benchmark, verification value depends on how unresolved evidence can affect the decision. The Rashomon model set, support-function bounds, and minimax-regret criterion make that relationship computable under the specified uncertainty model; versioned data updates carry the result into the research workflow.
